name: The Long Stride
unique_feature: an Oroth causeway whose hinge-less lamp posts light one after another at dusk
story: The Builders laid it to reach their foundation stone; the guilds charge a toll on it and pretend they built it.
encounter: cutpurses work the toll queue; a bravo duels anyone who refuses to pay

name: Shingle Shrine
unique_feature: a Hearthstone built of lake pebbles, each one a name scratched by a traveller
story: Travellers coming down out of the heights add a pebble here before the shore road to the city. The Tallymen tried to charge for it once; the pebbles were found in the guildmaster's bed.

name: North Cliff Beacon
unique_feature: a ruined beacon whose fire-bowl is an upturned Oroth bell
story: Lit only when the lake serpent was last seen, forty years ago. Smugglers use it now to signal the Undercroft.
encounter: smugglers with a dropout Sayer casting Hush; the cliff stair is the only way up unless you climb the drainage

name: The Gullhithe Wreck
unique_feature: a fishing smack broken on the shingle with gulls nesting in its nets
story: The Lamp went dark one night; the boat found the shore the hard way. The keeper says she was asleep. The gulls disagree.
encounter: gutter drakes in the hull; a smuggler's cache under the keel

name: The Eelweir
unique_feature: a wicker weir across the Mere's western outflow with a walkway of eel traps
story: Reedfolk and Lakefolk share the weir by an agreement neither has read. Every autumn someone is pushed in.
encounter: leech-hounds come up the channel at night

name: The Pilgrim Stair
unique_feature: Oroth steps that walk straight into the lake and keep going underwater
story: Nobody has counted the steps below the waterline and come back to say. A Sayer left a rope tied to the last dry one; it is still taut.
encounter: none above water; the sunken barge lies at the stair's foot

name: Willow Isle
unique_feature: an islet under a single pollarded willow the size of a barn, with a hermit's boat moored in its roots
story: The hermit Ivo Goslin was a Tallymen clerk who stopped counting. He will tell you the price of anything, correctly, and refuse to sell it.
encounter: none; a book and a side quest

name: The Bell Buoys
unique_feature: a line of twelve buoys whose bells ring in any wind, each tuned to a note of the Toll
story: The Sayers tuned them to prove the Bell account; on still nights they still ring, which proves nothing to anyone's satisfaction.
encounter: none; row out to hear the chord

name: The Limekilns
unique_feature: three kilns at the foot of the Whitecut burning its chalk into the lime that whitewashes Tollmere
story: Every white wall in the city began as the Vale's hill. The burners work the kilns in shifts and are paid by the Tallymen by weight, which is the one thing everybody agrees is fair.
hook: The lime from the third kiln has come out grey, and the Tallymen want to know whether they can still sell it.

name: The Narrows Bridge
unique_feature: an Oroth arch over the mouth of the Skerrow Water, the first thing the North Road crosses on its way out of the heights
story: Clan carters coming down Kharrow Gorge cross the Narrows Bridge into the Tallymen's country. The arch has a clan mark cut on its north side and a guild mark on its south, and neither side admits to the other.
hook: The clan mark and the guild mark were both chiselled off the Narrows Bridge in the same night.

name: Gull Holm
unique_feature: an Oroth pier-house on an islet in the Mere, white with the gulls that nest in its windows
story: Nobody lands on Gull Holm except Merrowhithe's egg-collectors, once a spring, and they come back quiet. The pier-house has a door with no hinges that faces the city.
hook: The egg-collectors bring back one egg a year that is warm, from a room with no nest in it.

name: The Strandline Stones
unique_feature: three stones on the highest of the Mere's old shorelines, marking where the water stood the year the Toll fell
story: The Mere has fallen ten metres since the Toll came down and left its old beaches up the hillside like steps. The Sayers say it is draining; the Lakefolk say it is resting.
hook: A Sayer's measuring-rod stands by the stones: the water fell a finger's width this spring, the first change in a century.

name: The Listening Post
unique_feature: a Sayers' listening-tower on the east shore with a brass horn turned toward Merrowby to take the Toll's hum across the water
story: Ismay Ondrael's figures come from here: the Circle has taken the pitch of the hum every night for forty-one years from a room with a horn, a chair and a clerk who cannot sing.
hook: The clerk says the hum changed pitch on the night the Foundling came up the Stair.

name: The Tallyman's Folly
unique_feature: a Tallyman's summer house abandoned half-built when the Charter changed, the unpaid masons' names cut into the lintel
story: Guildmaster Pellow began it in 998 and stopped the day building became a paid service under the Charter. The masons cut their names into the lintel instead of their bill, which the Quiet Hands call the best receipt in Tollmere.
encounter: cutpurses use the cellars after dark
hook: The masons' names on the lintel are a debt the Tallymen never closed, and the Quiet Hands want it copied before the lintel is recut.

name: The Rafters' Camp
unique_feature: a timber camp at the Wold Water's mouth where Briarwold logs are lashed into rafts for the city
story: The Woodfolk float down what they will sell and not a stick more; the rafters pole it across to Tollmere's timber quay and complain about the Woodfolk the whole way.
hook: A raft came down the Wold Water with a forester tied to it, alive, silent, and not saying who.

name: The Stair Bridge
unique_feature: a stone bridge over Rudd Beck built from the steps of a Builders' stair somebody took apart
story: The north shore road crosses Rudd Beck here. On a still night the stones are said to count themselves, one to forty, and stop.
hook: A Merrowhithe mason says the stair went up to something before it was a bridge, and wants to know what.

name: The Wash-Stones
unique_feature: a spring that comes up soft through the chalk into a kerbed wash-pool on the old shore, its water running down a stone runnel to the Mere; three flat stones set at the pool's lip where Tollmere's washing is beaten, each worn into a dish, and the guild's white drying on lines
story: Tollmere's laundresses come over the Stride twice a week because the water here is soft: it rises through the chalk under the old shore and lifts the grey out of linen as nothing in the city does. The stones are older than the city; the laundresses say the Builders did their washing too. Dorcas Pell beats the guild sheets on the middle stone, and on her way home walks out to the Tally Needle with a stub of chalk.
hook: A shirt came up in the wash that none of the laundresses brought: a Sayer's, with a name in the collar that the Circle unsaid.

name: The Sedge Hearth
unique_feature: a Hearthstone on a peat island in the reeds, reached by a single plank
story: Sedgehithe's cutters built it where the Lakefolk and the reedfolk quarrelled over the reed-beds, so that both would have to share one fire.
hook: The plank to the island has been taken up, from the island side.

name: The Dry Jetty
unique_feature: a boardwalk jetty standing in a hayfield two hundred yards from the water, where the Mere used to reach
story: Gullhithe's old landing, left high in one lifetime as the Mere fell. The eel-wives still walk out along it at dusk, from habit.
hook: Every morning this spring the jetty's last pile has been wet to the knee, and the field round it dry.

name: The Eggers' Camp
unique_feature: tents and rope-coils at the top of the Gull Cliffs, where Gullhithe's egg-collectors go over on ropes
story: Every spring Gullhithe goes over the cliff on ropes for the gulls' eggs, and every spring somebody's rope is found cut.
hook: This year the cut rope was cut from below.

name: The Charter Stone
unique_feature: the stone the first Charter was cut on, broken by the clans and mended with brass pins
story: Where the clans and the Tallymen agreed in 712 that the North Road would be free of toll above the Narrows and of blood-price below them. Both sides have broken it since, and both still come here to swear.
hook: The brass pins are being drawn out, one a night, and there are two left.

name: Brindle Mill
unique_feature: a clan grist-mill on Brindle Beck whose mill wheel turns against the water
story: Brindlecrag's lowland mill, where the clans grind the barley they buy from the Vale. The miller is clanless and pays nobody.
hook: The wheel turns against the current, and for a stride below the mill the beck runs uphill.

name: The Counting Tower
unique_feature: a Tallymen's tower where the North Road's carts were counted before the Charter freed the road, every window bricked but one
story: The Tallymen still keep a clerk here, counting the carts that come down out of Skerrow for a tax nobody has paid since 942.
hook: The clerk has stopped counting; the tower's ledger is being kept by someone else, in Oroth numerals.

name: The Standing Arches
unique_feature: a run of the Builders' aqueduct striding over the cliff-top toward Merrowhithe, broken at both ends
story: Water never ran in it in anyone's memory. Merrowhithe's smokehouses are hung in its last arches, down at the shore.
hook: The channel along its top is wet this spring from end to end, and drips at the break.

name: The Beached Barge
unique_feature: a Woodfolk timber barge the Mere left high and dry, with an oak growing up through its hold
story: Beached when the water fell in 1005, with her last cargo still lashed. Nobody has claimed the timber: the Woodfolk say it was never paid for and the Tallymen say it was never delivered.
hook: The oak growing through the hold is older than the barge.

name: The Log Boom
unique_feature: a boom of chained logs across the Wold Water, walked like a bridge by the rafters
story: The rafters make up their rafts behind the boom and let them go one at a time, so that the Mere is not all logs at once.
hook: A raft was let go with nobody on it, and it went up the Wold Water, not down.

name: The Lime Bridge
unique_feature: a whitewashed bridge over the Cressbourne's mouth, limed so often it is more lime than stone
story: The lime-burners whitewash it every spring with the first burn, for luck, and the Tallymen charge the kilns for the lime.
hook: This spring the bridge came up grey under the whitewash, like the third kiln's lime, and the white will not take.

name: The Heronry
unique_feature: a dead Oroth tower standing in the wet meadows above Sedgehithe, its top a city of herons' nests
story: The herons have held it as long as anyone has held anything on the Mere. The Tallymen tried to tax the eggs once, and the clerk came back without his hat.
hook: The herons have left all at once, in the middle of the nesting, and flown west.

name: The Net Field
unique_feature: a field of eel-nets drying on poles behind Gullhithe, with the net-menders' shelter in the middle
story: Gullhithe mends its nets here in the wind off the fen. The menders can tell a Mere knot from a Sedgish one by feel in the dark, and cut the Sedgish ones out.
hook: A net came back from the water mended with Sedgish knots, by nobody in Gullhithe.

name: The Smoke Coppice
unique_feature: a coppicers' camp in the oak coppice cut for Merrowhithe's smokehouses, the stools older than the Charter
story: Merrowhithe smokes its pike over oak from here and nowhere else, and pays the coppicers in fish, which they say is the only honest wage on the Mere.
hook: One stool has put up a shoot overnight as thick as a man's arm, and the coppicers will not cut it.

name: The Larkmouth Bridge
unique_feature: a stone bridge over the Larkbourne's mouth with a bench on it facing the city
story: The Larkbourne's last crossing before the Mere. The Vale's old men walk down on fine evenings to sit on the bench and say what they think of Tollmere, across the water, where it cannot hear.
hook: Somebody sits on the bench every night until dawn, and the old men will only say that he is waiting for the city's lamps to go out.

name: The Ness Market
unique_feature: a fish market of trestles and awnings on the Stride Ness, the land side of the causeway, where the boats land their catch
story: Lakefolk fishers sell here because a fish sold on the Ness pays no city toll. The Tallymen have been trying to move the toll-line out to the Ness's root for forty years.
encounter: none; Bryony Kettle selling the morning's catch off her trestle, and Silas Pask entering it as it passes his line of white stones
hook: The Tallymen have put a clerk at the Ness's tip overnight, with a ledger and no warrant.

name: Skarl Mill
unique_feature: a clan mill of dry-stone and turf on the Skarl Water below Merrowhithe, its wheel paddled with giants' rib-slivers
story: The Skarl Mill grinds oats for three clans, each on its own day, and keeps three hoppers so that no clan's grain touches another's, which is a blood-price matter.
hook: The three hoppers were found mixed one morning, and all three clans are waiting to hear whose fault it was.

name: The Carters' Rest
unique_feature: a carters' bench of split oak on a flagged plinth where the charcoal road tips down to Merrowhithe, and a cairn of soot-black stones beside it looking out over the Mere
story: The charcoal carts from the Smoke Coppice stop here to rest the horses before the long drop to the shore. Every carter adds a stone to the cairn with a black thumbprint on it, for luck on the brake.
encounter: a hired bravo stops the charcoal carts at the brow and asks a fee
hook: Every morning this month there has been a white stone on top of the cairn, Vale chalk, and nobody on this road carries chalk.

name: The Charter's End
unique_feature: a squat boundary waystone a pace off the North Road, the Charter's scales cut on its lake face and a clan chain-link on its fell face, the ground worn bare on both sides of it
story: The Charter's writ runs to this stone and blood-price begins beyond it. A Tallymen's bailiff will not serve a writ north of it and a clan will not claim a death south of it, so debtors of both sides have been known to live out their lives within a stride of it.
encounter: the debtor has friends: two cutpurses on the fell side at dusk
hook: A debtor has sat against the fell face every night this month, a stride out of the Charter's reach, and the bailiff with his writ sits against the lake face, and they have started sharing a pipe.

name: The Drovers' Trough
unique_feature: a drovers' fire beside a long stone trough where the clan herds are watered before the Narrows, with hurdles stacked for a night pen
story: Every herd driven down the North Road to Tollmere's market is watered here and rested a night before the bridge. The Counting Tower's clerk walks over at dawn to count the beasts for a tax nobody pays, and the drovers give him breakfast for the entertainment.
hook: The trough was found brimming with salt water one morning, and every beast that drank from it that day has refused the Narrows Bridge since.

name: The Forgiving Stones
unique_feature: a heap of lake pebbles round a standing stone in sight of the Counting Tower, each pebble scratched with a sum of money somebody forgave, the newest on top still wet from the shore
story: A ledger has no column for forgiveness, the lakefolk say, so they keep it here. A creditor who lets a debt go carries a pebble up from the shore, scratches the sum on it and adds it to the heap in sight of the Counting Tower, which is the point.
encounter: a cutpurse picks the pockets of those who kneel at the heap
hook: A pebble has been laid scratched with the Counting Tower's own mark and the sum of the North Road tax unpaid since 942, and the tower's clerk swears the Tallymen forgive nothing.

name: The Fair-Day Stone
unique_feature: a milestone on the shore road cut with one notch for every market held at Kharrow Foot, the rows of nicks running down both faces into the grass
story: Lowland carters notch the stone on their way up to every market at Kharrow Foot, so that the clans cannot say a market was missed. The clans keep their own count on a stick at the market's bell-post, and the two counts have never once agreed.
encounter: on market eves cutpurses walk up the road behind the carters
hook: The stone has one notch more than the bell-post's stick, cut fresh, for a market the clans say was never held.

name: The Withy Camp
unique_feature: an eel-trappers' camp on the bank of Rudd Beck, withy traps stacked by the fire and a smoking-rack of split willow
story: Merrowhithe's trappers set their withies in Rudd Beck from the Stair Bridge down to the shore and sleep out beside them, because an eel trap left unwatched on the North Shore is a gift to the next man along.
hook: Every trap on the beck came up full the night the Toll hummed, and the eels in them were the blind white eels from under the Mere, which nobody has ever caught in running water.

name: The Three Rights
unique_feature: three carved stones in a row by the shore road, each cut with its sign: a fish for the right to net, a cup for the right to draw water, a foot for the right to pass
story: Gullhithe and Brindle Mill settled their quarrel over the beck mouth with three stones and three rights, and have argued ever since about which stone is which. Travellers only need the third.
encounter: two of the Beacon's smugglers watch the shore road from the stones after dark
hook: Somebody keeps setting a fourth stone in the verge beside them, uncarved, and every morning Gullhithe has dragged it out and rolled it into the Mere.

name: The Lamp Niche
unique_feature: a waystone with a lamp-niche hollowed in its road face and blackened with soot, facing the ruined beacon on the cliff
story: The niche was cut to hold a lamp for carters feeling their way along the shore road in fog. The smugglers who use the North Cliff Beacon use the niche too: a light in it tells the beacon that the road is clear of the Watch. The smugglers keep a Tollmere crossbow wrapped in oilcloth behind the stone, for nights the Watch comes early.
hook: The niche was lit last night and the beacon answered it, and every smuggler on the Mere swears the light was not theirs, at either end.

name: Hesper's Boat
unique_feature: a lake-boat dragged far up from the water and left on her side by the road, broken open, her hold made into a shelter with a chest under the standing ribs
story: When the Mere took Hesper Wick's husband she had his boat dragged uphill as far from the water as six Gullhithe men would pull it, and lived in the wreck for thirty years with her back to the lake.
hook: Hesper died at midwinter, and since then somebody has been mending the boat's planking at night, strake by strake, as if she meant to be launched.

name: The Listener's Tent
unique_feature: a Sayers' listening camp by the Stair road, a tent with a writing-board and a line of tuning tines hung in the wind toward the lake
story: The Circle keeps a listener here through the summer to hear the rope on the Pilgrim Stair. A taut rope hums, the Sayers hold, and whatever holds the other end of it hums with it; the listener writes down the note.
hook: The note the rope hums has changed, and the listener packed her tent to carry the news to the Spire herself and left half her papers behind.

name: The Salt Barn
unique_feature: the roofless stone salt-barn at the Narrows where the Salt Isles' salt was stored for the clans, one gable still standing and the floor still white
story: Salt came up the Mere from the Salt Isles traders and was sold to the clans here for curing their mutton. The barn has stood empty since Kharrow Foot started selling salt itself, and its floor has never stopped being white.
encounter: smugglers use the barn after dark: a smuggler-Sayer and a cutpurse
hook: The barn floor was found swept, and a line of salt laid across its doorway from post to post, the way the reedfolk lay it against the drowned.

name: The Serpent Watch
unique_feature: a watchers' cairn on the shore bank facing the Mere, a flat stone on its top worn into a seat by forty years of sitting
story: When the serpent was last seen, forty years ago, Gullhithe set a watch on the bank here, and every watcher added a stone at the end of his night. The watch was given up. The cairn was not.
hook: A stone has been added to the cairn every night since the Toll hummed, and each one is wet and weeded, as if it came up out of the Mere.

name: The Unsayers' Stones
unique_feature: three short weathered stones in the verge below Kharrow Gate where travellers who would not say the clans' law back are sent to wait the night
story: The gate-ward tells every traveller the law and asks them to say it back. A traveller who will not is not turned away, only sent down to the stones to sit the night and think, and let up at dawn to try again.
hook: There has been a woman waiting at the stones every dawn this month who will not give a name, and she is gone before the gate-ward comes down.

name: The Pike Shrine
unique_feature: a roadside shrine where Merrowhithe hangs the first smoked pike of the season on a hook over the stone, for whoever is walking hungry
story: Merrowhithe has no opinion about anything, the city says, and it is wrong about one thing: the first fish out of the smoke belongs to the road, and whoever is hungry on it takes the fish and says nothing.
encounter: down-wolves come for the pike on the hook after dark
hook: The first pike has been taken three mornings running and a clan bone token left on the hook in its place, a different clan's every morning.

name: The Reeve's Chair
unique_feature: a stone chair by the shore road with a hawthorn grown up through its back, where a reeve sat to hear the shore's disputes before the Charter came
story: Before the Charter the North Shore had a reeve who sat by the road and settled what the fishermen could not. The last reeve died in the chair, and the hawthorn came up through its back the spring after, and nobody has sat to judge since.
hook: Somebody sat in the chair all of last Tollday under the hawthorn and heard disputes, and the whole shore has kept the judgements, and nobody saw their face.

name: The Burner's Clamp
unique_feature: a charcoal-burner's camp by the Skarl Water with a turf-covered kiln smoking beside the road and the burner's lean-to of cut poles
story: The charcoal for Merrowhithe's smokehouses is burned here from the Smoke Coppice's oak. A clamp must smoulder and never flame, so the burner sits up with it for the ten nights it takes, and walks round it every hour, and talks to it.
encounter: down-wolves drawn by the smoke circle the clamp at night
hook: The clamp has been smouldering for forty days without being fed, and the burner will not open it.

name: Market Brow
unique_feature: a cairn on the brow where the road up from the shore first shows Kharrow Foot's walled market-field below
story: Lowland traders going up to market leave a stone on the cairn and take one away again on the way down. A trader who comes down with no stone to take has lost more at Kharrow Foot than he meant to, and everyone on the road can see it.
hook: Every stone taken down from the cairn after the last market has been brought back up this week and piled at its foot, and every one of them has been split clean in two.

name: The Dodgers' Stone
unique_feature: a waystone at the Lake Road's fork where carters turn off to go round the Stride's Foot weighbridge, a cart-wheel scratched on it and a finger pointing the back way
story: Everything that goes to Tollmere on wheels is weighed and priced at Stride's Foot, unless it goes round by the shore, which is slower, muddier and free. The finger was scratched by a carter long ago. The Tallymen have had it chiselled off four times.
encounter: two cutpurses wait at the fork for carters dodging the weighbridge
hook: Somebody has chiselled the pointing finger round to face the weighbridge, and the Tallymen swear it was not them.

name: The Laundry Punt
unique_feature: a laundresses' punt dragged up the bank of the Lake Road and left on her side, broken open, a line of washing-pegs still along her rail
story: Before the Stride's Foot road was mended, Tollmere's washing came across the water in this punt twice a week for the Wash-Stones. When the laundresses started walking over the causeway the punt was dragged up the bank and left, and nobody has the heart to burn it.
encounter: a cutpurse works the Lake Road on washing days
hook: The punt has been found full of wet washing every morning, beautifully folded, shirts and shifts that nobody in Tollmere owns.

name: The Rafters' Knots
unique_feature: a shrine on the east shore road where the rafters leave a knot of rope on the stone for every raft that reached the city whole
story: A raft of Wold timber poled across the Mere to Tollmere's timber quay comes whole or comes in pieces, and the rafters give the Mere a knot for every one that came whole. The stone is furred with rope ends like an old dog.
hook: A knot has been left on the stone for a raft that nobody at the camp launched.

name: The Salvagers' Fire
unique_feature: a salvagers' fire on the east shore where the Mere's driftwood is sorted, good timber stacked to one side and the rest burned
story: The Mere gives up timber from every broken raft and every beached barge, and the salvagers sort it on the shore: good oak for Tollmere's yards, the rest for the fire. Nobody salvages from the Beached Barge; the timber there is argued over.
encounter: a smuggler-Sayer comes ashore at dusk to trade, and not always to trade
hook: The salvagers found a barge's name-board in the drift, freshly painted, with the Beached Barge's name on it.

name: The Old Shore Bench
unique_feature: a bench on a flagged plinth on the old shore road where the Mere once lapped, a cairn of lime-white stones beside it, looking over the water at Tollmere
story: The Mere has fallen ten metres since the Toll came down, and left its beaches up the hill like steps. The old folk of Stride's Foot sit on the bench where their grandparents paddled and say the water is resting, whatever the Sayers say.
encounter: down-wolves come down to the old shore to drink after dark
hook: The water has been seen at the bench's feet at dawn, lapping where it has not lapped for forty years, and gone again by breakfast.

name: The Weight Stone
unique_feature: a waystone by the lime road with a hollow cut in its top where the burners weigh a sample basket of lime against the Tallymen's iron
story: The lime-burners are paid by weight, which everybody agrees is fair, and the weight is taken here on the road where both sides can watch, with the Tallymen's own iron in the stone's hollow and the burners' own basket beside it.
hook: The Tallymen's iron has been found in the hollow three mornings running, and each morning it weighs a pound less.

name: The Hum Cairn
unique_feature: a lone cairn on the east shore road with a brass tuning fork bedded in its top stone, set by the Listening Post's clerk
story: The clerk at the Listening Post cannot sing, and so cannot hold the Toll's note in his head between nights. He bedded a fork in the cairn tuned to the hum, and strikes it on his way to work to know what he is listening for.
encounter: a hired bravo waits by the cairn after dark for the Listening Post's clerk
hook: The fork has been humming on its own at night, the Toll's note, a quarter-tone sharp.

name: The Toll Rope
unique_feature: a cutpurses' camp beside the shore road, a rope strung across the way and a hat on a stick for the toll
story: The Charter freed the North Road of tolls in 942. Nobody told the cutpurses of Merrowhithe's shore, who string a rope across the road on fine days and take a penny a head, which is less than the Tallymen took and more honest about it.
encounter: two cutpurses take a toll at the rope by day
hook: The toll has gone up to a name: travellers are asked for one they do not use any more, and the cutpurses write it down.

name: The False-Light House
unique_feature: a roofless boat-house on the shore road where wreckers once showed false lights to the rafts, one gable standing toward the water
story: Before the Log Boom let the rafts out one at a time, the Mere was all logs in a south wind, and men in this boat-house showed lamps to draw rafts onto the shallows and took the timber. The Tallymen hanged two of them and the rest took up smuggling, which paid better.
encounter: a smuggler-Sayer shows a lamp from the boat-house after dark
hook: A lamp has been shown from the gable after dark, the old wreckers' signal, and a raft that nobody launched came in on the shallows below it.

name: The Eggers' Cairn
unique_feature: a gulls' cairn on the cliff path over the shore road, built by the Gullhithe eggers to mark the nests they may take from
story: Gullhithe's eggers take gulls' eggs from the cliff every spring and leave the nests past the cairn alone, so the colony goes on. A boy who takes past the cairn is sent out in the boat at dawn to put an egg back.
hook: Every nest on the eggers' side of the cairn was empty this spring, and every nest past it had one egg more than it should.

name: The Old Shoreline Cairn
unique_feature: a cairn of lake-rounded stones on the Mere's old shoreline above Sedgehithe, built at the water's edge the year the Toll fell and left high and dry
story: The Mere has fallen ten metres since the Toll came down, and this cairn was built at its edge that year, by fishermen marking a good landing. It stands in a meadow now, a long walk from any water, and the herons stand on it.
hook: There was a wet line round the cairn's foot at dawn this week, exactly where the water stood when it was built.

name: The Burners' Spring
unique_feature: a spring-trough of whitewashed stone below the Limekilns, a tin cup on a chain, the only sweet water on the lime shore
story: Lime dust gets into everything on the Whitecut shore, the Mere's edge included, and the burners drink from the one spring that comes up clean, a walk down from the kilns. The Tallymen charge the kilns for the lime and have never found a way to charge for the spring.
hook: The cup on its chain has been found full of lime-water every morning, milk-white, and nobody at the kilns will drink from the spring now.

name: Pennyfold Keep
unique_feature: a square lime-washed customs fort on the south-west shore, its yard the pen where the Tallymen once folded the south road's goods overnight to be counted, a brass lamp still lit over its gate
story: Pennyfold was the Tallymen's customs fort for the south shore when the south shore had a toll: every bale and barrel off the Sedgehithe road was penned in its yard overnight and counted in the morning. The Charter of 998 made the road free, and the fort was sold, at a fair price, to its only bidder: the Fair Company, bravos out of Tollmere, who now sell the road's travellers writs of protection from themselves, witnessed and sealed, at a fair price.
encounter: the Fair Company's cutpurses and bravos on the walls and in the yard, crossbows on the corner towers, and their captain, Sabeline Marr, in the counting-vaults under the keep
hook: A charter-board by the gate prices the Company's protection by the mile, in a clerk's good hand, and the Tallymen's old seal is still painted at its head because nobody told the painter to take it off.

site.hook_prompt: Read the charter-board by the gate

name: The Bleaching Green
unique_feature: a green on the south shore where Tollmere's guild linen is bleached: rows of white cloth stretched on tenter-frames in the hard light, lye-tubs steaming, and a bleachers' hut with a brass lamp lit whenever the cloth is out overnight
story: The guilds' linen, the Tallymen's ledger-cloth and the Sayers' white all come here to be bucked in lye, stretched on the frames and watered for a fortnight until the Mere's light has taken the colour out of them. Linnet Whitlow has kept the green for thirty years under a charter that makes her answerable for every ell. This spring the Fair Company rode over from Pennyfold and sold her a writ of protection, and they take a bolt a week against it.
encounter: none; the bleachers at work, the Company's writ nailed to the hut door, and day-work posted for jobs on the green's notice post
hook: One frame stands bare: the Company took its cloth, a Sayer's white, and Linnet is answerable for it to the Circle.

name: The Hush Hole
unique_feature: a cleft in the North Fen's low cliff breathing cold still air, where no sound carries past the third step in, with a slide of greased planks running down into it from the fen for boats
story: The Builders called it Hesk-Ondr, the deep silence, and cut nothing in it; the Mere did the cutting when it stood higher. The smugglers call it the Hush Hole, because the Spire's dropouts who work it have Hushed its throat: a word said inside does not reach the fen. Goods come up the channels from Sedgemire by night, are knotted into Mere nets to pass the Gullhithe boats, and go down into the Hole to wait for the Undercroft's buyers.
encounter: smugglers and a Hushed sayer at the mouth by night; inside, cutpurses in the wet halls, sayers on the ledges, and the Word-Seller, Ambrose Quell, at the landing under the cliff
hook: An eel-net hung to dry across the mouth, every knot in it Sedgish, with a Gullhithe float still on its head-rope.

site.hook_prompt: Look at the net over the mouth

name: The Cadbrae Slate Cut
unique_feature: a slate quarry cut into the east shore's brae in grey steps, split slates stacked by the thousand on the benches, and in the deepest face a course of black stone that is not slate and hums when the wind is in the east
story: Every roof in Tollmere is Cadbrae slate, split along the grain by the Slades, who have cut this brae for six generations under a Tallymen's charter that pays by the thousand. Last autumn the cut reached a course of black Oroth stone laid through the hill like the footing of a wall, and the slate that comes away against it hums in the hand.
encounter: cutpurses after dark, sent to prise a singing slate out of the face for a buyer in the Undercroft
hook: Barnet Slade has set one humming slate aside on the splitting-bench, wrapped in sacking, and will not sell it to anyone who comes asking for it at night.

name: The False Lantern
unique_feature: a lamp-post of drift timber on the lip of the North Fen with a brass lantern that shows only to the water, its landward panes blacked with pitch
story: An honest lamp on the Mere shows all round. This one was put up to bring boats in under the fen cliff to the Hush Hole, and its landward panes were pitched so that nobody in Gullhithe would see it lit. The keeper of the Lamp has written to the Tallymen about it four times, and been charged for the paper.
encounter: a smuggler's boy trims it on moonless nights, and does not like to be seen doing it
hook: The oil in its reservoir is the Lamp's own oil, which is not sold.

name: The Priced Gibbet
unique_feature: a lime-washed gibbet on the west shore with a brass price-plate screwed to its arm, the figure on the plate scratched out and cut again eleven times
story: Tollmere's charter lets a thief taken outside the walls be hanged where he was taken, on payment of the hanging-fee, and the fee is on the plate. It has risen with the price of rope. Nobody has hanged on it in thirty years: the Quiet Hands pay whoever is due to hang more than the fee to go on living, and the Tallymen collect the fee from the Hands instead, which everyone agrees is better accounting.
encounter: cutpurses at dusk, come to pay their respects
hook: The twelfth figure has been cut on the plate, and it is lower than the eleventh.

name: The Weed-Cutters' Hut
unique_feature: a reed-thatched hut on the west shore with long-handled weed-scythes racked along its wall and a punt drawn up on the shingle, where the men who keep the Eelweir channel clear of lilies sleep in the season
story: The Mere's waterlilies choke the channel down to the Eelweir every summer, and the Tallymen pay two Sedgehithe men by the rod to cut them. The lilies grow back in a night whatever is done to them, and lately they have begun to grow back in rows.
encounter: none; the cutters are out on the water by day
hook: The cutters' tally of rods cut has a second column beside it, in a hand neither of them writes, counting something else.

name: The Thousand Post
unique_feature: a tall post above the east shore's slate-landing, notched once for every thousand slates sent down to the boats, six generations of notches climbing it past a man's height, the highest cut from a ladder
story: The Slades notch the post when a thousand slates leave the landing for Tollmere, and the Tallymen's boatman counts the notches against his ledger when he pays. They have never once agreed. The post is older than the ledger, and the Slades say it is the only honest count on the east shore.
hook: Last autumn's notches are cut deeper than the rest, in a hand none of the Slades will own to, and there are more of them than slates went down.

name: The Crown Drift
unique_feature: a calamine mine on the North Shore's upper terrace: a timber headframe with its winding-wheel over the shaft, a roofless engine-house beside it with a tall stone chimney, and a spoil heap of grey-green waste the colour of verdigris spilling down toward the Mere; the brass of every lamp in Tollmere, and of the crown on the Sayers' Spire, came up out of it
story: The Tallymen sank the Crown Drift in 860 for the calamine that turns copper into brass, and for a hundred and fifty years every brass lamp on the Mere came up its shaft, and the crown on the Sayers' Spire with them. In 1012 the deep level broke through into a gallery that was already there: square, black, cut by the Builders, the ore in it lying dressed and stacked as if for collection. The shift-captain took eight men down to bring it up. None of them came back up the ladder, and the Tallymen entered the drift in their ledger as closed, no further value. The shift-board at the shaft head still has nine tokens missing from it. Lately somebody is bringing brass up again, by night, and nobody in Gullhithe hears a pick.
encounter: brass-takers at the shaft head after dark; below, the takers working the old levels in a Hushed silence with a smuggler-sayer to keep it, gutter drakes in the warm stope, and on the Builders' level the nine who went down in 1012, still on their shift, and their captain at the board
hook: A shift-board at the shaft head with a hook for every man's token, and nine hooks empty since 1012; somebody keeps the board's paint fresh.

site.hook_prompt: Read the shift-board at the shaft head

name: The Struck Barrow
unique_feature: the Tally Needle, a lime-washed obelisk four times a man's height with a brass cap that catches the sun across the Mere, standing at the mouth of a gully in the south shore's scarp; every name the Charter struck off is cut on its faces and struck through with one chisel line, and at the gully's head a dressed stone portal goes into the hill
story: Under the Charter a debtor who dies owing is struck off the city's Roll, and a man struck off is nobody's to bury. The Tallymen built the Struck Barrow into the south shore's scarp in 740 to receive them: no names inside, only numbers, and outside the Needle, where each name was cut once so that it could be struck through. Four thousand lines. The Receiver who kept the barrow was struck himself in 1019, the post's fees being owed, and the barrow was shut. Since then the struck have been seen at the Needle's foot at dusk, reading. And somebody has been chalking names back over the struck lines.
encounter: resurrection men from the Undercroft at the portal by night, come for names the dead are not using; inside, the struck on their shelves, a bailiff who never stopped distraining, and the Receiver at his register
hook: Names chalked back over the struck lines at the Needle's foot, in a laundress's careful capitals, as high as a woman can reach.

site.hook_prompt: Read the names on the Needle

name: Holmwatch
unique_feature: a broken castle of five drum towers on the east shore's promontory, facing Gull Holm across the water, its curtain torn down on the lake side, and over it the Reeves' lamp-tower, a tall round tower with an iron cage at its head where the reeve's light burned before the Lamp at Gullhithe was lit; at dusk something sings in it louder than the gulls
story: The Lake-Reeves held the Mere from Holmwatch before there was a Charter: they judged the shores, kept the reeve's light on the lamp-tower, and took their dues in kind at the water-gate under the promontory. The Charter of 712 made judging a paid service and the Reeves had nothing to sell; the last of them died in his chair on the north shore road, and the castle was given to the Sayers' Circle as a listening-seat until the Spire was crowned. The Circle left it. This spring the Loud took it: Sayers put out of the Spire for Saying too loud, who hold that the world is going quiet because nobody will speak up, and who have been Saying from the lamp-tower every dusk since, so loud that the Listening Post across the water cannot hear the Toll.
encounter: the Loud's acolytes and their hired bravos on the walls and in the yard, Loud Sayers on the towers; under the keep the Reeves' halls, the cellars and the water-gate where the drakes come in, and Magister Ysolde Carrow in the Saying-hall at the bottom
hook: A Sayer's speaking-trumpet of brass nailed to the gate-arch mouth outward, and under it, chalked in letters a hand high: LOUDER.

site.hook_prompt: Read what is chalked under the trumpet on the gate

name: The Sounding Mirror
unique_feature: a dish of black Oroth stone twelve metres across standing on edge on the brow of the north shore, hollowed like the inside of a bell and turned to face Tollmere across the Mere, and in front of it, at the point where the hollow gathers sound, a waist-high speaking-stone with a brass ear-cup worn bright
story: The Builders cut the Mirror to hear the city they built, and it still does: stand at the speaking-stone and whatever is said loud enough on the far shore arrives in the cup, small and clear, as if it were said at your shoulder. The Sayers' Circle kept a listener here until the Spire was crowned. Now the Quiet Hands keep one: Mab Larrow, who has sat at the stone for nine years with her eyes shut and a slate on her knee, and who sells what the Mere says to whoever pays, a line at a time.
hook: Mab Larrow sits at the Sounding Mirror on the north shore's brow and sells what the city says across the Mere, a line at a time; put your ear to the cup and you can hear it yourself, for free, if you can stand what you hear.

name: The Ropewalk
unique_feature: a shed fifty paces long and two wide, open-sided on lime-washed posts under a single slate roof, running along the south shore with three strands of rope stretched down the whole length of it on T-stakes, the jack-wheel at one end and the weighted sledge at the other, a tar-copper smoking by the door
story: Every rope on the Mere is laid here, and every one the Charter buys has a red yarn twisted into its heart, the rogue's yarn, so that a stolen fathom can be known by cutting it. Absalom Tarr has walked the walk backwards for forty years, paying the hemp out of the bundle round his waist while his boy turns the jack, and has laid enough rope to go round the Mere eleven times. He lays a fathom for anyone who walks the top home with him, for luck, and lately someone has been asking him to lay rope with no red in it.
hook: At the Ropewalk on the south shore Absalom Tarr lays the Charter's rope with a red yarn in its heart; someone who will not give a name has asked him for sixty fathom without it.

name: The Widows' Keels
unique_feature: three lake-boats hauled up the south-west shingle and turned keel-up for houses, tarred black, with doors cut in their sterns and stovepipes through their bottoms, eel-racks smoking between them and a tall board on two posts by the water chalked with the names of boats that did not come home
story: When a lake-boat comes home without its skipper, the Lakefolk will not sail her again and will not burn her. She is hauled up and turned over, and whoever was left at home lives under her. Grisel Mew has lived under the Hope of Sedgehithe for twenty-two years and smokes eel for Tollmere's tables under the other two, and keeps the drowned-board: every boat lost off this shore since the Charter, chalked up, and never rubbed out until the boat or its people are found. Her son's is the newest name on it.
hook: Grisel Mew keeps the drowned-board at the Widows' Keels on the south-west shore; her son's boat, the Merry Tally, is the newest name on it, and she has heard it was seen tied up somewhere it should not be.

name: The Charter Scale
unique_feature: a beam-balance big enough to weigh a boat: a timber gantry twelve metres high on the south shore west of the Stride's Foot with a black beam across its head on a brass pivot, chains from each end to a pan of planks the size of a barge's deck, one pan grounded under a stack of iron weights and the other swung up in the air
story: Before the Stride had a toll-gate there was the Scale: every boat coming to Tollmere by the south shore was lifted on to its pan, cargo and all, and the Charter's toll taken on the weight. The Tallymen moved the toll to the city gate a hundred years ago and left the Scale standing, because nobody would pay to take it down. Prudence Gauge, the last Weighmaster, never left with it. She weighs whatever the shore brings her, a pig, a cart of slate, a quarrel between two brothers, and she keeps the beam true with weights that nobody else can lift the right way.
hook: Prudence Gauge, the Weighmaster of the Charter Scale on the south shore, says the salt coming down from the Saltmound weighs four stone light a barge, every barge, and wants somebody who can count to go and see why.

name: The Cormorant Perches
unique_feature: two staggered rows of tall T-shaped perches along the south-east shore, each with a black cormorant on its crossbar holding its wings out to dry like a hung coat, a reed shelter, a flat boat drawn up and a creel of fish; at dusk the whole row turns its heads to the water at once
story: Corbin Vell fishes with birds. He takes them as chicks from the Gull Cliffs, rings their throats with copper so they cannot swallow the big fish, and they dive for him off the punt and bring up what the Mere has, which is pike, and sometimes other things: a ring, a key, a Tallyman's seal off a drowned purse. The Tallymen fined him for fishing without a net-licence and he paid in pike. He has fourteen birds and names them all after taxes.
hook: Corbin Vell's cormorants dive off the south-east shore and bring up whatever the Mere has; he will tell you, if you ask, what else they carry when they fly across the water at dusk.

name: The Kite-Fishers' Shore
unique_feature: a row of heavy reel-posts on the east shingle below the Wold Water's mouth, each paying a line up into the wind to a kite of oiled silk hanging over the water, painted with a pair of staring eyes to frighten the pike up, and from every kite a baited dropper trailing down to the Mere
story: The east wind comes down out of the Briarwold and goes out over the Mere, and Gullhithe's poorest worked out a long time ago that a kite will carry a baited line further out than any boat they could not afford. Dilly Fane, who is eleven and has the steadiest hands on the shore, flies her mother's kites now her mother is in the Undercroft for debt; she pays the reel-tax in fish and keeps the rest. On a good wind the eyes over the water can be seen from the city.
hook: On the east shingle below the Wold Water's mouth the kite-fishers fly painted eyes out over the Mere; Dilly Fane lets anyone take a turn on a reel for a share of whatever bites.

name: The Dumb Fair
unique_feature: a ring of tall black poles on the south-east shore hung with screens of tarred sailcloth like a crown of shadows, hooded lanterns on hooks between them, and inside, round a flat stone with a felt-wrapped bell on it, trestles of salt sacks, crates and covered baskets that nobody stands behind by day
story: Nothing at the Dumb Fair is said aloud. It is held every night of the year in the ring of screens, which the Free Salters set up a lifetime ago because a word said on the Mere's shore can carry to the Listening Post; so the trade is done in fingers and chalk, and a price is a number of knocks on the trestle. Untaxed salt, rope with no red in it, Hush sayings in sealed jars. The Tallymen know where it is. Everyone knows where it is. Nobody has ever heard it.
hook: A fair is kept every night behind black screens on the south-east shore where nothing is said aloud and nothing is taxed; the woman who keeps it is called the Hush-wife, and she trades in knocks.

name: The Saltmound
unique_feature: a cone of grey-white salt as high as a church heaped on the west shore, the Charter's tithe of the Salt Isles' trade, with a barrow-trestle running up its flank to the summit and the Tallymen's brass seal-pole on its top; at its foot a lime-washed salt-gate with brass-bound doors sealed with the Charter's wax, and round the back, toward the water, a timbered cut where somebody has been digging into it
story: Every tenth sack of salt that comes over the Grey Sea from the Salt Isles is the Charter's, and has been since 712; it is heaped on the west shore under seal, weighed in by the Tallymen and sold out to the city by the barge, and the Saltmound has stood there white so long that the gulls nest on it. Obed Marrow, the salt-reeve, has kept the seals for thirty years and swears none has been broken. None has. The Free Salters do not come in through the gate. They have been tunnelling into the mound's heart from the water side for years, carving galleries in it and carrying the Charter's salt out to the Dumb Fair a sack at a time, and the man who runs them, Hesketh Vane, has made himself a hall in the middle and calls himself the Salt-King.
encounter: two Free Salters loading a boat at the cut after dark; inside, the Salters in their galleries, a Hushed sayer to keep them quiet, drakes at the brine, and the Salt-King on his throne of sacks in the heart of the mound
hook: A tithe-board by the Saltmound's sealed gate, kept by the salt-reeve: every sack in and every barge out for thirty years, and in the last column, in another hand, a running total that does not agree.

site.hook_prompt: Read the tithe-board by the salt-gate

name: Fathom Shears
unique_feature: a sheer-legs of two ship's masts twenty metres high on Tollmere's west tail, leaning out over the Mere with a chain running down from its head into the water, and on the stone quay beneath it the salvors' diving bell, the Patience, a black iron bell as tall as two men, set on its cradle with its mouth open to the ground
story: Tollmere stands on Builders' stone, and so does the floor of the Mere west of it: the Drowned Quarter, streets and halls the Builders raised before the water came, still standing forty fathom down. The Fathom Company holds the Charter's licence to salvage it, and for sixty years has lowered the Patience into it off the west tail and raised bronze, bells and black stone by the ton. Below, they say, the Quarter is dry: the Builders' note holds the water off its halls like a held breath. Three weeks ago Master Corwen Lisle took the bell down with four men after the Undersong, the Quarter's great bell, and the Patience came up on the chain with nobody in it, ringing.
encounter: at night, the drowned salvors walk up the quay steps out of the Mere and stand round the bell; inside, the Quarter's flooded halls, the held salvors at their work, drakes in the dry vaults, and Corwen Lisle in the bell-hall, striking the Undersong
hook: A salvors' slate hung on the windlass at Fathom Shears, with the Patience's last dive chalked on it: down at the sixth hour, five men; up at the ninth, none; and under it, every hour since, a mark for each time the chain has rung.

site.hook_prompt: Read the salvors' slate on the windlass
